\chapter{Songs and Stories}
\label{ch:ml-arts}
\hlchaptermodality{99}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a song, singing, dance and a story.}

From cold: the four arts words, and the three different things an ending does to the word in front of it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pāṭṭŭ]{\ml{പാട്ട്} (pāṭṭŭ) — a song}

\label{lesson:ML-C99-paattu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is a good film}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} — \emph{pāṭṭŭ} — \textbf{a song.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{നല്ല} \ml{പാട്ടാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ nalla pāṭṭāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}This is a good song.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Listen to the join and you will hear nothing arrive.} \textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} ends in the breathed half-u, and the chapter before this one told you what those do when an ending comes: they step aside and let it land.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{joined to \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{നല്ലത്}} & \textbf{\ml{നല്ലതാണ്}} (\emph{nallatāṇŭ}) \\
\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} & \textbf{\ml{പാട്ടാണ്}} (\emph{pāṭṭāṇŭ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{You have done this before without a new word to do it on.} \textbf{\ml{നല്ലതാണ്}} has been in the book since the opinion chapter. \textbf{\ml{പാട്ടാണ്}} is the same event on a word you met a moment ago — no \textbf{\ml{യ}}, no \textbf{\ml{വ}}, nothing inserted.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pāṭṭŭ}
  \item \emph{itŭ nalla pāṭṭāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{nallatāṇŭ}, then \emph{pāṭṭāṇŭ}, and hear that neither gains a letter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{a song}? (\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}}.) What slides in before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{Nothing} — \textbf{\ml{പാട്ടാണ്}}.) And why not? (\textbf{It ends in the half-u, not a full vowel}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāṭuka]{\ml{പാടുക} (pāṭuka) — to sing}

\label{lesson:ML-C99-paaduka}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a song}. Then say \emph{to play}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{പാടുക}} — \emph{pāṭuka} — \textbf{to sing.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പാടുന്നു}.} — \emph{ñān pāṭunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}I sing.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Last chapter the noun sat inside the verb. This pair is not built that way.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{verb} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കളി}} & \textbf{\ml{കളിക്കുക}} — the noun is there whole \\
\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} & \textbf{\ml{പാടുക}} — the \textbf{\ml{ട്ട}} thins to a single \textbf{\ml{ട}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say them one after the other and you will hear it: \textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} holds the \textbf{ṭ} long, \textbf{\ml{പാടുക}} does not.

\textbf{Two words, one pattern between them — and that is all it is.} The book has put other nouns beside their verbs — \textbf{\ml{വായന}} beside \textbf{\ml{വായിക്കുക}}, \textbf{\ml{ചോദ്യം}} beside \textbf{\ml{ചോദിക്കുക}} — and not one of them does this. \textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}}/\textbf{\ml{പാടുക}} is the only pair in the book where the consonant itself changes weight.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pāṭuka}
  \item \emph{ñān pāṭunnu}
  \item \emph{pāṭṭŭ}, then \emph{pāṭuka}, and hear the long \textbf{ṭ} shorten
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{to sing}? (\textbf{\ml{പാടുക}}.) What is \emph{a song}? (\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}}.) What happens to the \textbf{\ml{ട്ട}} in the verb? (\textbf{It thins to a single \ml{ട}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nṛttaṁ]{\ml{നൃത്തം} (nṛttaṁ) — dance}

\label{lesson:ML-C99-nrttham}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a song}. Then say \emph{beautiful}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{നൃത്തം}} — \emph{nṛttaṁ} — \textbf{dance.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{നല്ല} \ml{നൃത്തമാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ nalla nṛttamāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}This is a good dance.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{This is the third join, and the one the book explained to you first.} \textbf{\ml{നൃത്തം}} ends in the \textbf{\ml{ം}}, and you have known since the good-and-bad chapter what that sign does when \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} arrives: it is already the \textbf{m}, and it takes the full letter \textbf{\ml{മ}} so it can carry the vowel behind it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word ends in} & \textbf{joined to \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}} \\
\midrule
the half-u & \textbf{\ml{പാട്ടാണ്}} (\emph{pāṭṭāṇŭ}) \\
\textbf{\ml{ം}} & \textbf{\ml{നൃത്തമാണ്}} (\emph{nṛttamāṇŭ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Two words, two different endings, and neither one gains a sound.} The first gives one up; the second only changes how its \textbf{m} is written.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nṛttaṁ}
  \item \emph{itŭ nalla nṛttamāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{pāṭṭāṇŭ}, then \emph{nṛttamāṇŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{dance}? (\textbf{\ml{നൃത്തം}}.) What does its \textbf{\ml{ം}} become before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{\ml{മ}} — \textbf{\ml{നൃത്തമാണ്}}.) And does the \textbf{m} sound change? (\textbf{No} — only its writing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[katha]{\ml{കഥ} (katha) — a story}

\label{lesson:ML-C99-katha}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a film}. Then say \emph{dance}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{കഥ}} — \emph{katha} — \textbf{a story.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{നല്ല} \ml{കഥയാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ nalla kathayāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}This is a good story.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{You have a word that ends exactly as this one does.} \textbf{\ml{കഥ}}'s last letter is \textbf{\ml{ഥ}}, carrying its own \textbf{\ml{അ}} — and \textbf{\ml{സിനിമ}} ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}} too. So the same \textbf{\ml{യ}} slides in:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ends in} & \textbf{word} & \textbf{joined to \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അ}} & \textbf{\ml{സിനിമ}} & \textbf{\ml{സിനിമയാണ്}} (\emph{sinimayāṇŭ}) \\
\textbf{\ml{അ}} & \textbf{\ml{കഥ}} & \textbf{\ml{കഥയാണ്}} (\emph{kathayāṇŭ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{That is the whole chapter in three words.} \textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} gives a sound up, \textbf{\ml{നൃത്തം}} re-spells one, and \textbf{\ml{കഥ}} takes a letter in — three endings, three outcomes, and you were told each one before you met the word it lands on.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{katha}
  \item \emph{itŭ nalla kathayāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{sinimayāṇŭ}, then \emph{kathayāṇŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{a story}? (\textbf{\ml{കഥ}}.) \textbf{\ml{കഥ}} ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}} — what slides in before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{\ml{യ}} — \textbf{\ml{കഥയാണ്}}.) Which word you already had does the same? (\textbf{\ml{സിനിമ}} — \textbf{\ml{സിനിമയാണ്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāṭṭuṁ kathayuṁ enna ōrmma]{(a song, singing, dance, a story) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R99-arts-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{a song}, \emph{to sing}, \emph{dance}, \emph{a story}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three endings, three different events}]
Five words met \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} in this chapter and the one before, and \textbf{the three endings did three different things}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{joined to \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}} & \textbf{what happened} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} & \textbf{\ml{പാട്ടാണ്}} (\emph{pāṭṭāṇŭ}) & ends in the half-u — a sound is \textbf{given up} \\
\textbf{\ml{നൃത്തം}} & \textbf{\ml{നൃത്തമാണ്}} (\emph{nṛttamāṇŭ}) & ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}} — the \textbf{m} is \textbf{re-spelled} \\
\textbf{\ml{കഥ}} & \textbf{\ml{കഥയാണ്}} (\emph{kathayāṇŭ}) & ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}} — a \textbf{\ml{യ}} is \textbf{added} \\
\textbf{\ml{സിനിമ}} & \textbf{\ml{സിനിമയാണ്}} (\emph{sinimayāṇŭ}) & ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}} — a \textbf{\ml{യ}} is \textbf{added} \\
\textbf{\ml{കളി}} & \textbf{\ml{കളിയാണ്}} (\emph{kaḷiyāṇŭ}) & ends in \textbf{\ml{ഇ}} — a \textbf{\ml{യ}} is \textbf{added} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Given up, re-spelled, added} — three different events, and the only thing that tells you which you are looking at is \textbf{how the word ended}. Note the last two rows: \textbf{\ml{അ}} and \textbf{\ml{ഇ}} are different vowels and both call for \textbf{\ml{യ}}, so it is the particular vowel that decides, not vowel-hood on its own.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} is the song; \textbf{\ml{പാടുക}} is doing it. Unlike \textbf{\ml{കളി}} and \textbf{\ml{കളിക്കുക}}, the noun is not sitting whole inside the verb — the long \textbf{ṭṭ} thins to a single \textbf{ṭ}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പാടുന്നു}.} — \emph{ñān pāṭunnu} — I sing.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pāṭṭŭ}, \emph{pāṭuka}, \emph{nṛttaṁ}, \emph{katha}
  \item \emph{itŭ nalla pāṭṭāṇŭ}, then \emph{itŭ nalla kathayāṇŭ}
  \item which of the four rows gives a sound up, and which adds one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A song, dance, a story? (\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}, \ml{നൃത്തം}, \ml{കഥ}}.) Which of the three \textbf{gives a sound up} before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{\ml{പാട്ട്}} — it ends in the half-u.) And which \textbf{adds} one? (\textbf{\ml{കഥ}} — it ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}}, so a \textbf{\ml{യ}} comes in.)
\end{tcolorbox}
